children.text: This capstone brings the course together into one exercise. You will define a transformation portfolio, sequence it by dependency, find its binding constraint, check its capital against its gates, model what a slip would do, build its risk register and benefits trace, and finish with a one-page portfolio brief that answers the oversight question from Lesson 14.

Use a real organization if you can: your hospital, your agency, your state or a program you know well. If you cannot, use Vermont's portfolio as Chapter 15 records it; the platform's tools load it as a preset. Allow three to four hours, in one or two sittings.

Every step uses a platform tool, and each tool corresponds to a row of Chapter 15's Work This Chapter on the Platform table. By the end you will have done, at small scale, the core work of a portfolio office.
Step 1: Define and Sequence the Portfolio

Begin with the inventory method from Lesson 3. List every component with a named owner and a dated obligation, assign each to one pillar, and record its type, priority, lead and next stage gate. Then open the Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test, replace the Vermont preset with your components, and set each component's status and whether its implementation needs the pillar's upstream gate.

Score the five pillars' current readiness and read the verdicts. Note which components are correctly waiting, which are late by dependency order, which are running ahead of a closed gate, and which unfinished components the test identifies as the places where schedule pressure belongs. Compare that list with where your organization's attention actually is today.

If you are using Vermont's portfolio with the Fall 2026 scores, you should find twelve components on track, the RHT Program deployment running ahead of its gate, three components late by dependency order, and the four Technology components as the pressure points. If your results differ, check the gate settings before the scores.

children.text: Step 2: Find the Binding Constraint and Check the Capital

Open the Transformation Friction Index at /transformation-friction-index and score your organization or state on each pillar. Chapter 15 notes that the tool finds the binding constraint by sensitivity rather than by the highest bar: the pillar whose improvement would lift delivered readiness most is where the portfolio manager's attention belongs. Then list your three most urgent initiatives by deadline. If none sits in the binding-constraint pillar, your portfolio is being scheduled by calendar rather than by dependency.

Next, open the Investment Tracker at /investment-tracker and use the portfolio check to enter your components' committed capital by pillar. The tool checks each against its pillar's limiting gate and flags components funded ahead of their upstream gate. The book calls money moving faster than dependency order the early signal of premature investment.

Record three facts from this step: the binding-constraint pillar, whether your most urgent initiatives sit in it, and which components are funded ahead of their gate. These become the centre of your portfolio brief.

If the two tools disagree, for example the Friction Index names Technology while your capital is concentrated in Economics, that disagreement is the finding. It usually means money is following deadlines or sponsors rather than the dependency chain.
The binding constraint is found by sensitivity, not by the weakest score. Ask which pillar's improvement would lift delivered readiness most; that is where the next dollar and the next hour belong.
Step 3: Model a Slip and Score the Portfolio

Open the HTR Simulator at /htr-simulator, enter your pillar scores, and lower the binding-constraint pillar by fifteen points. Watch the downstream pillars fall with it. Then use the Impact Simulation at /impact-simulation to model what a single component slipping does to the rest of the portfolio and identify the components with no slack, the ones whose slip moves other pillars' outcomes.

Then score the portfolio the way an outside reviewer would, using the Transformation Scorecard at /research-lab/knowledge-workspace?tab=scorecard. Chapter 15 makes a pointed observation about this step: divergence between what the portfolio office reports and what the scorecard shows is itself a governance finding. If your own status reports describe the portfolio as healthier than the scorecard does, note where and why.

If you have a Subscriber plan, the HTI Dashboard at /hti-dashboard shows Vermont's five-pillar status moving over time rather than at a single date, which is the trend a monthly report cannot show. Use it to compare your portfolio's direction of travel with Vermont's.

children.text: Step 4: Register the Risks and Trace the Benefits

Build a risk register using Lesson 10's format. Start with the pressure points and the no-slack components from the first three steps: each is a risk to everything that depends on it. Add structural risks to the mandate, funding, capacity and engagement. Score each on a fixed probability and impact scale, choose a response, and name an owner. Then read the register as Lesson 11 does: plot it, group risks by shared cause, and check which can be reduced by work that is unblocked today.

Build the benefits trace from Lesson 12. List the goals your transformation serves, map every component to at least one, and choose a lagging measure with a target and a date, plus a leading measure, for each goal. Flag components that serve no goal and goals that no component serves.

Together, the register and the trace complete the picture: what the portfolio contains, in what order it must run, what threatens it, and what it is for. That is the information a governance body needs and rarely receives.

body.message: It is tempting to leave the most uncomfortable risks off a register you will show to others, especially risks about leadership, capacity or political will. Chapter 15's own register puts the absence of the portfolio function at the top. An honest register is the only useful one.
body.title: Keep the register honest

children.text: Step 5: Write the One-Page Portfolio Brief

Finish with a one-page brief for your governance body. Open with the answer to the oversight question: which component is the binding constraint, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it. Follow with the sequencing findings, components running ahead of their gate and components late by dependency, and the capital funded ahead of its gate.

Then give the two or three risks that need a decision now, each with options and the cost of not deciding, and a benefits summary showing whether each goal is on course. Close with the management infrastructure the portfolio needs, costed as a share of what it coordinates and tied to the risks it reduces, as in Lesson 13.

If you can write that page with confidence, you have done what Chapter 15 argues Vermont, and most organizations running a transformation, have not yet done: managed the transformation as a portfolio. Revisit the brief quarterly. The binding constraint will move, and the brief is how you will know.

Share the brief with the people who own the components as well as with the governance body. Component leads who see the whole portfolio, its binding constraint and its top risks understand why their own component is being accelerated, held back or resourced differently, and they become the first line of the portfolio's early-warning system. A portfolio brief that only travels upward manages the governance body; one that also travels outward manages the portfolio.

points: The capstone runs the core work of a portfolio office end to end on a real or Vermont portfolio.
The Portfolio Sequencing Test turns the inventory into verdicts and identifies where schedule pressure belongs.
The Friction Index finds the binding constraint by sensitivity, and the Investment Tracker's portfolio check flags capital funded ahead of its gate.
The HTR Simulator and Impact Simulation show how a slip propagates and which components have no slack.
Divergence between internal status reporting and the Transformation Scorecard is itself a governance finding.
The risk register and benefits trace complete the picture of what the portfolio contains, threatens and is for.
The one-page brief opens with the oversight answer: the binding constraint, its owner and what would accelerate it.

body.explanation: Chapter 15's Try This exercise makes exactly this comparison. If urgency is driven by deadlines that all fall outside the binding-constraint pillar, attention and resources are going where the calendar points rather than where the dependency logic says delivered readiness is being held back.

options.text: That the Friction Index is miscalibrated for your organization
That the portfolio is being scheduled by calendar rather than by dependency, the failure the chapter is written to prevent
That the binding constraint does not need attention until its deadline
That the portfolio has no dependencies

body.question: In Step 2 you find that none of your three most urgent initiatives by deadline sits in the binding-constraint pillar the Friction Index identifies. What does Chapter 15 say this indicates?
